unit-alg-t2-06.title: Topic 2 · 2-6 The Quadratic Formula
unit-alg-t2-06.source: enVision Algebra 2 Lesson 2-6: The Quadratic Formula

cards.def:
**x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ⁄ 2a — solves any equation in the form ax² + bx + c = 0.**
• It works even when the equation can't be factored.
• It comes from completing the square on the general equation ax² + bx + c = 0.
cards.hint: This formula NEVER fails — it works on every quadratic equation, factorable or not.

cards.def:
**The expression under the square root in the Quadratic Formula: b² − 4ac.**
• Its value — without even finishing the formula — tells you how many solutions there are and what kind.
• It's called the discriminant because it discriminates (distinguishes) between the different cases.
cards.hint: You don't need to solve the whole equation to know the discriminant — just plug into b² − 4ac.

cards.def:
**Two distinct real solutions.**
• The square root of a positive number is a real number, and the ± splits it into two different values.
• Graphically, the parabola crosses the x-axis at two separate points.
cards.hint: Positive discriminant, positive square root, two real answers.

cards.def:
**Exactly one real solution.**
• The square root of 0 is 0, so the ± doesn't create two different values — it's just one.
• Graphically, the parabola's vertex sits exactly ON the x-axis, touching it at one point.
cards.hint: When the discriminant is 0, the ± has nothing left to split.

cards.def:
**Two complex (non-real) solutions.**
• The square root of a negative number is imaginary, so both solutions come out complex.
• Graphically, the parabola never touches the x-axis at all.
cards.hint: Negative discriminant means the graph never reaches the x-axis — the solutions exist, just not as real numbers.

cards.def:
**Identify a, b, and c, substitute carefully (parentheses help with negative numbers), then simplify.**
• A common error is losing a negative sign when substituting a negative b or c.
• Simplify the square root and reduce the fraction fully at the end.
cards.hint: Write out a, b, and c explicitly before substituting — it catches sign errors before they happen.

cards.def:
**Factoring is fastest when an equation factors easily; the Quadratic Formula always works, even when it doesn't.**
• Completing the square is most useful when you need vertex form anyway.
• All three methods give the exact same solutions — they're different tools for the same job.
cards.hint: There's no WRONG method here, only faster and slower ones for a given equation.

cards.def:
**In an application, a negative discriminant means the situation described in the problem never actually happens.**
• A ball "reaching a certain height" becomes a quadratic equation — if its discriminant is negative, the ball never reaches that height.
• Checking the discriminant first can answer a yes/no question without solving the whole equation.
cards.hint: Sometimes the discriminant alone answers the question — no need to find the actual solutions.

cards.def:
**For 2x² − 5x − 12 = 0: a = 2, b = −5, c = −12, giving x = −3/2 or x = 4.**
• Discriminant: (−5)² − 4(2)(−12) = 25 + 96 = 121, a perfect square.
• A perfect-square discriminant means the solutions come out as clean fractions, not messy radicals.
cards.hint: A perfect-square discriminant is a sign this equation could have been factored instead.

questions.q: What is the Quadratic Formula?
questions.hint: There's a minus sign on b, and the denominator is 2a.
steps: The Quadratic Formula solves ax² + bx + c = 0 for x.
It has the specific shape x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.
Each detail matters: minus b, minus 4ac under the root, and 2a in the denominator.

ex.main: **x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a.** Every piece of this formula is load-bearing — change any sign and it breaks.

questions.q: What is the discriminant of a quadratic equation?
questions.hint: It's the expression under the square root sign in the formula.
steps: The discriminant is defined as the part of the Quadratic Formula under the radical.
In x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / 2a, that part is b² − 4ac.
So the discriminant is b² − 4ac.

questions.q: What are the solutions of 2x² − 5x − 12 = 0?
questions.hint: Identify a, b, and c, then substitute into the Quadratic Formula.
steps: Identify: a = 2, b = −5, c = −12.

ex.main: **x = −3/2 and x = 4.** A perfect-square discriminant (121 = 11²) is why these solutions come out as clean fractions.

questions.q: What is the discriminant of x² − 4x − 1 = 0, and how many real solutions does that mean it has?
questions.hint: Compute b² − 4ac first, then decide what its sign means.
steps: Identify: a = 1, b = −4, c = −1.
Compute the discriminant: (−4)² − 4(1)(−1) = 16 + 4 = 20.
20 is positive, so the equation has two distinct real solutions.

ex.main: **20, two real solutions.** A positive discriminant that ISN'T a perfect square still means two real solutions — they just involve a square root that doesn't simplify to a whole number.

questions.q: What are the solutions of x² + 2x + 5 = 0?
opts: x has no solutions at all
questions.hint: Compute the discriminant first — expect a negative number.
steps: Identify: a = 1, b = 2, c = 5. Discriminant: (2)² − 4(1)(5) = 4 − 20 = −16.
Since the discriminant is negative, the solutions are complex: x = (−2 ± √−16) / 2 = (−2 ± 4i) / 2.
Simplify: x = −1 + 2i and x = −1 − 2i.

ex.main: **x = −1 ± 2i.** Every quadratic equation has exactly two solutions — when the discriminant is negative, they're just complex instead of real.

questions.q: An equation has a discriminant of 0. How many real solutions does it have?
questions.hint: The ± in the formula needs a nonzero square root to actually create two different values.
steps: When the discriminant is 0, the square root term is √0 = 0.
The formula becomes x = (−b ± 0) / 2a, and adding or subtracting 0 gives the same result either way.
So there's exactly one real solution, not two.

ex.main: **Exactly one.** The ± only produces two different answers when there's something nonzero to add and subtract.

questions.q: An equation has a discriminant of −16. What does this tell you about its graph?
opts: The parabola never crosses or touches the x-axis
The parabola touches the x-axis at exactly one point
The parabola crosses the x-axis at two points
questions.hint: A negative discriminant means the solutions are complex, not real.
steps: A negative discriminant means the equation has two complex solutions and no real ones.
Real solutions are exactly the x-values where the graph crosses the x-axis.
With no real solutions, the graph never crosses OR touches the x-axis at all.

ex.main: **The parabola never crosses or touches the x-axis.** No real zeros means no x-intercepts, full stop — the sign of a says nothing about that.

questions.q: A ball's height is modeled by h(t) = −5t² + 20t + 3, where t is time in seconds. Will the ball reach a height of 25 feet?
opts: No — the discriminant of −5t² + 20t − 22 = 0 is negative
Yes — the discriminant of −5t² + 20t − 22 = 0 is positive
Yes — the ball starts at 3 feet, which is close to 25
No — the ball's maximum height is exactly 3 feet
questions.hint: Set the height equal to 25, rearrange to standard form, then check the discriminant.
steps: Set h(t) = 25: −5t² + 20t + 3 = 25, which rearranges to −5t² + 20t − 22 = 0.
The discriminant is negative, meaning there's no real solution — the ball never reaches 25 feet.

ex.main: **No, the discriminant is negative.** Checking the discriminant answers the yes/no question directly, without ever solving for an actual time.

questions.q: What value(s) of b will cause 3x² + bx + 27 = 0 to have exactly one real solution?
questions.hint: One real solution means the discriminant equals exactly 0.
steps: For exactly one real solution, set the discriminant to 0: b² − 4(3)(27) = 0.
Simplify: b² − 324 = 0, so b² = 324.
Take the square root of both sides: b = ±18.

ex.main: **b = 18 or b = −18.** Setting the discriminant to exactly 0 and solving for the unknown is how you work BACKWARDS from "how many solutions" to the coefficients.

questions.q: What are the solutions of x² − 6x + 9 = 0?
questions.hint: Check the discriminant first — it may simplify the whole problem.
steps: Compute the discriminant: (−6)² − 4(1)(9) = 36 − 36 = 0.
A discriminant of 0 means there's exactly one real solution.
Using the formula: x = −(−6)/(2(1)) = 6/2 = 3.

ex.main: **x = 3.** A discriminant of 0 always signals a perfect-square trinomial — this one is (x − 3)².

questions.q: Without fully solving, how many real solutions does 4x² − 12x + 9 = 0 have?
opts: None, since it doesn't factor obviously
questions.hint: Just compute the discriminant — you don't need to go further to answer this.
steps: Compute the discriminant: (−12)² − 4(4)(9) = 144 − 144 = 0.
A discriminant of exactly 0 always means exactly one real solution.
So this equation has one real solution — the sign of a and c don't decide this, only the discriminant does.

ex.main: **One, since its discriminant is 0.** The discriminant alone answers "how many" — you never needed to find the actual solution to know that.

questions.q: Rick claims x² + 5x + 9 = 0 has no solutions, while Jenny claims it has two solutions. How can they both be right?
opts: Rick means no REAL solutions; Jenny means two COMPLEX solutions — both statements are true
One of them made an arithmetic error and is simply wrong
The equation genuinely has no solutions of any kind, so Jenny is wrong
The equation has two real solutions, so Rick is wrong
questions.hint: Check the discriminant — a negative one supports both claims at once, in different senses.
steps: Compute the discriminant: 5² − 4(1)(9) = 25 − 36 = −11.
A negative discriminant means there are no REAL solutions — which is what Rick is saying.
But every quadratic equation still has exactly two solutions when complex numbers are allowed — which is what Jenny is saying. Both are correct, just using "solutions" differently.

ex.main: **Both are right — Rick means real solutions, Jenny means complex ones.** "No solutions" and "two solutions" only conflict if you assume both people mean the same number system.

questions.q: What is the discriminant of 3x² − 20x − 7 = 0, and how many real solutions does that indicate?
questions.hint: Compute b² − 4ac carefully with the given values.
steps: Identify: a = 3, b = −20, c = −7.
484 is positive, so the equation has two real solutions.

ex.main: **484, two real solutions.**

questions.q: A rock is thrown from a 6-foot wall, modeled by h(t) = −16t² + 32t + 6, where t is time in seconds. Will the rock reach a height of 24 feet?
opts: No — the discriminant of −16t² + 32t − 18 = 0 is negative
Yes — the discriminant of −16t² + 32t − 18 = 0 is positive
Yes — 24 is less than the rock's starting height plus its speed
No — the rock's maximum height is below 6 feet
questions.hint: Set h(t) equal to 24, rearrange to standard form, then check the discriminant.
steps: Set h(t) = 24: −16t² + 32t + 6 = 24, which rearranges to −16t² + 32t − 18 = 0.
The discriminant is negative, so there's no real time at which the rock is at 24 feet — it never reaches that height.

ex.main: **No, the discriminant is negative.**

questions.q: Why is the Quadratic Formula useful even for equations that could be solved by factoring?
opts: It works on every quadratic equation, including ones that don't factor with integers
Factoring only works on equations with a discriminant of 0
It's the only method that gives real solutions
questions.hint: Think about what happens when an equation genuinely can't be factored.
steps: Factoring only works cleanly when integer or simple fractional factors exist.
Many quadratic equations don't factor nicely at all — their solutions involve irrational or complex numbers.
The Quadratic Formula solves ALL of these, factorable or not, which is why it's the one method that never fails.

ex.main: **It works on every quadratic equation, including ones that don't factor.** That's the formula's whole reason for existing — universality, not speed.

questions.q: What is the discriminant of 5x² + 4x + 3 = 0?
questions.hint: Watch the signs carefully — every term here is positive.
steps: Identify: a = 5, b = 4, c = 3.

ex.main: **−44.** All-positive coefficients don't guarantee a positive discriminant — 4ac can still outweigh b².

questions.q: Sage used the Quadratic Formula on x² − 3x − 2 = 0 and got x = (3 ± √17)/4, but neither solution satisfies the original equation. What is Sage's error?
opts: The discriminant should have been calculated as −17, not 17
b should have been substituted as −3, not 3
There is no error — the Quadratic Formula does not always work
questions.hint: Check the formula's denominator against the actual value of a.
steps: The Quadratic Formula's denominator is 2a, and here a = 1, so the denominator should be 2(1) = 2, not 4.
Sage's error was writing 4 in the denominator instead of the correct 2 — the formula itself never fails when applied correctly.

ex.main: **The denominator should be 2a = 2, not 4.** The Quadratic Formula is completely reliable — an answer that doesn't check out means an arithmetic slip, not a limitation of the formula.

questions.q: An equation has a = 2 and a discriminant of 0. If b = 8, what is the equation's one real solution?
questions.hint: With a discriminant of 0, the formula simplifies to just −b/2a.
steps: When the discriminant is 0, the Quadratic Formula reduces to x = −b/(2a), since the square-root term vanishes entirely.

ex.main: **x = −2.** A discriminant of 0 means the ± term disappears completely, leaving just −b/2a — the same formula that finds a vertex's x-coordinate.

questions.q: For the equation −x² + 3x − 8 = 0, what are the correct values of a, b, and c to substitute into the Quadratic Formula?
questions.hint: Match each coefficient to its term, including its sign.
steps: Match the equation −x² + 3x − 8 = 0 to the standard form ax² + bx + c = 0.
The coefficient of x² is −1, the coefficient of x is 3, and the constant is −8.
So a = −1, b = 3, and c = −8.

ex.main: **a = −1, b = 3, c = −8.** Missing the negative sign on a is one of the most common substitution errors — writing it out explicitly before substituting catches it.

questions.q: Which method is generally fastest for solving x² + 4x − 12 = 0?
opts: Factoring, since it factors easily as (x + 6)(x − 2)
The Quadratic Formula, since it always works
Graphing, since it's the most visual
questions.hint: Check whether the equation factors with small integers first.
steps: Check for factors: two numbers that multiply to −12 and add to 4 are 6 and −2.
Since it factors cleanly as (x + 6)(x − 2) = 0, factoring solves it in one step: x = −6 or x = 2.
The Quadratic Formula would give the same answer, just with more arithmetic — factoring is faster here specifically because this equation happens to factor easily.

ex.main: **Factoring.** All three methods always agree on the answer — the question is only ever about which is fastest for THIS particular equation.
